Erdős problem #243

Reciprocal-tail rigidity near the Sylvester recurrence

Under a rapid-growth hypothesis on an integer sequence, does rationality of its reciprocal sum force the sequence to satisfy the Sylvester recurrence eventually?

Results and open questions

#243. Under the exact cubic rate 𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1 =1 +3/𝑛 +𝑜(𝑛−3)an2/an+1=1+3/n+o(n−3), every strictly increasing positive integer sequence has an irrational reciprocal sum. Lean checks the zero-indexed theorem through a square-specialisation argument using Mathlib’s Dedekind-zeta simple pole; the short paper transfers it to one-based indexing by an ordinary finite-prefix argument. Its printed proof uses classical Chebotarev instead. This rate does not cover the unrestricted Sylvester-tail question.

More generally, the nonintegral regular-rate theorem checks irrationality when 𝜆 >1λ>1 is nonintegral and 𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1 =1 +𝜆/𝑛 +𝑜(𝑛−𝜆)an2/an+1=1+λ/n+o(n−λ). Its Lean statement derives convergence for a positive, strictly increasing sequence indexed from zero. The long paper gives the ordinary finite-prefix transfer to one-based indexing. The integer-extraction lemma rules out nonintegral coefficients; the separate cubic argument rules out coefficient three. No rational examples are asserted for the remaining integer coefficients.

The rounded sequence 𝑎1 =8a1=8, 𝑎𝑛+1 =⌈𝑛𝑎2𝑛/(𝑛 +3)⌉an+1=⌈nan2/(n+3)⌉ has precisely this rate and product-ratio increments of order 𝑛2n2. Thus the separate bounded-increment recurrence criterion below gives no conclusion for it, while the cubic-rate theorem proves its reciprocal sum irrational. Duverney’s Corollary 3.2 supplies an earlier signed recurrence criterion under its printed one-sided growth-defect condition. In the all-positive, absolutely summable specialisation, the product-ratio increments tend to zero. For the rounded example, 𝑎𝑛+1/𝑎2𝑛 −1 ∼ −3/𝑛an+1/an2−1∼−3/n, so its signed defect series diverges and that absolutely summable specialisation does not apply. The exact 𝑜(𝑛−3)o(n−3) remainder matters to the polynomial-exclusion proof. These comparisons locate the contribution without deciding its novelty or priority; the short paper’s argument and example give the proof and source locators.

The short paper also proves an ordinary original-sequence corollary. Let 𝑎1 <𝑎2 <⋯a1<a2<⋯ be positive integers, 𝑎𝑛+1/𝑎2𝑛 →1an+1/an2→1, ∑1/𝑎𝑛∑1/an rational, and 𝑃𝑛 =∏𝑗<𝑛𝑎𝑗Pn=∏j<naj. If lim sup(𝑃𝑛/𝑎𝑛)(𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1 −1) < +∞lim sup(Pn/an)(an2/an+1−1)<+∞, then 𝑎𝑛+1 =𝑎2𝑛 −𝑎𝑛 +1an+1=an2−an+1 eventually. The needed limsup bound, or the paper’s alternative weighted record budget, is not proved for the unrestricted problem. Take a positive denominator 𝑞q of the full reciprocal sum and clear the nth tail by qP_n. The resulting integer error is minus 𝑞q times the scaled defect, up to a term tending to zero.

This cancellation turns the upper bound in the original sequence into the lower bound on the integer error used below. The proof passes through a signed bounded-negative theorem. Lean checks that theorem and the canonical tail transfer described below. Let a,C,D : ℕ → ℕ and E : ℕ → ℤ. Assume 𝑎(𝑛) >1a(n)>1, 𝐶(𝑛) >0C(n)>0, the exact recurrences 𝐶(𝑛 +1) +𝐷(𝑛) =𝑎(𝑛)𝐶(𝑛)C(n+1)+D(n)=a(n)C(n) and 𝐷(𝑛 +1) =𝑎(𝑛)𝐷(𝑛)D(n+1)=a(n)D(n), and that 𝐸(𝑛)E(n) is the exact centered state with |𝐸(𝑛)| <𝐶(𝑛)|E(n)|<C(n). If one constant 𝐵B satisfies 𝐸(𝑛) ≥ −𝐵E(n)≥−B for every 𝑛n, and for every 𝐾K one eventually has 𝐾|𝐸(𝑛)| <𝐶(𝑛)K|E(n)|<C(n), then 𝐸(𝑛) =0E(n)=0 eventually (boundedNegativePart_eventually_zero).

The checked centered-zero theorem then gives the Sylvester recurrence once the exact product-cleared orbit has an eventually nonzero next-tail state. Lean carries that chain to the original denominators in boundedNegativePart_sylvesterNext_eventually, and checks the LCM-weighted bounded-defect corollary from the rational reciprocal sum in original_coordinate_lcm_bounded_defect (ErdosProblems/Erdos243/PaperCompleteR7/LcmDefect.lean:49); the paper derives the displayed 𝑃𝑛Pn form from that corollary by 𝐴𝑛|𝑃𝑛An|Pn. For the state-system endpoint, no uniform lower bound on the centered error is proved.

Unbounded negative excursions and the full Erdős endpoint remain open. The signed recovery develops Koizumi’s canonical-tail framework under an additional bounded-negative premise. Read the short paper, long record, or selected formal checks.

The long record also proves an exact maximal-gap theorem for a separate static sieve. Let 𝑚0 <𝑚1 <⋯m0<m1<⋯ be pairwise coprime integers at least 22, with ℓ(𝑚𝑗) =𝑗 +𝑂(1)ℓ(mj)=j+O(1) for ℓ(𝑥) =log2⁡log2⁡max(4,𝑥)ℓ(x)=log2⁡log2⁡max(4,x). If 𝜎 =∏𝑗(1 −1/𝑚𝑗) >0σ=∏j(1−1/mj)>0 and 𝑢𝑛un lists the positive integers divisible by none of the 𝑚𝑗mj, then lim sup(𝑢𝑛+1 −𝑢𝑛)/ℓ(𝑢𝑛) =1/𝜎lim sup(un+1−un)/ℓ(un)=1/σ. Lean checks the general theorem maximal_gap_limsup_eq_inv_sigma with the convergence to 𝜎σ stated explicitly. The paper’s finite-product calculation gives 𝜎 =1/2σ=1/2 and thus coefficient 22 for the Fermat moduli 𝑚𝑗 =22𝑗 +1mj=22j+1. This concerns avoidance of whole moduli, not coprimality to composite moduli or construction of a reciprocal-tail orbit; the unrestricted #243 question remains open.

Introduction

The Sylvester recurrence 𝑎𝑛+1 =𝑎2𝑛 −𝑎𝑛 +1an+1=an2−an+1 gives a rational reciprocal sum by telescoping:

1𝑎𝑛−1=1𝑎𝑛+1𝑎𝑛+1−1.1an−1=1an+1an+1−1.

For an increasing sequence of positive integers that eventually satisfies this recurrence, the tail sum at every sufficiently large index is 1/(𝑎𝑛 −1)1/(an−1). Erdős and Graham asked whether every rational reciprocal sum with 𝑎𝑛+1 ∼𝑎2𝑛an+1∼an2 arises in this way.

Problem 1.1 (Erdős Problem 243). Let 1 ≤𝑎1 <𝑎2 <⋯1≤a1<a2<⋯ be a sequence of integers with

lim𝑛→∞𝑎𝑛𝑎2𝑛−1=1and∑1𝑎𝑛∈ℚ.limn→∞anan−12=1and∑1an∈Q.

Then 𝑎𝑛 =𝑎2𝑛−1 −𝑎𝑛−1 +1an=an−12−an−1+1 for all sufficiently large 𝑛n.

Erdős and Graham [5] asked this question; see also Erdős [6] and Bloom’s catalogue [11]. We prove the following irrationality result for a restricted class of sequences with 𝑎𝑛+1 ∼𝑎2𝑛an+1∼an2.

Theorem 1.2 (cubic-rate irrationality). A strictly increasing sequence of positive integers with

𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1=1+3𝑛+𝑜(𝑛−3)an2/an+1=1+3n+o(n−3)

has irrational reciprocal sum.

The eventual Sylvester recurrence gives 𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1 −1 =𝑂(1/𝑎𝑛)an2/an+1−1=O(1/an), far smaller than 3/𝑛3/n. Thus Theorem 1.2 rules out rationality in this subclass; none of our arguments treats the general quadratic limit alone.

For example, set 𝑎1 =8a1=8 and

𝑎𝑛+1=⌈𝑛𝑎2𝑛𝑛+3⌉.an+1=⌈nan2n+3⌉.

This gives 8,16,103,5305,…8,16,103,5305,…. From 𝑎𝑛+1 ≥𝑎2𝑛/4an+1≥an2/4 we obtain 𝑎𝑛 ≥4 ⋅22𝑛−1an≥4⋅22n−1 by induction. The error introduced by the ceiling is less than one, and hence

0≤1+3𝑛−𝑎2𝑛𝑎𝑛+1<16𝑎2𝑛=𝑜(𝑛−3).0≤1+3n−an2an+1<16an2=o(n−3).

The theorem applies to this explicitly defined sequence.

Rationality supplies a positive integer tail numerator 𝐶𝑛Cn, but not a bounded one: here it grows cubically. We therefore apply integrality to its finite differences. The exact comparison sequence 𝐹𝑛 =𝑛(𝑛 +1)(𝑛 +2)Fn=n(n+1)(n+2) has 𝐹𝑛+1/𝐹𝑛 =1 +3/𝑛Fn+1/Fn=1+3/n. The precision in the hypothesis forces Δ4𝐶𝑛 →0Δ4Cn→0, hence eventual equality 𝐶𝑛 =𝐴𝐹𝑛 +𝐵Cn=AFn+B. This extraction uses the numerator ratio and integrality, not the exact denominator recurrence.

The denominator recurrence now becomes decisive. It imposes a square condition at every root of a cubic modulo almost every prime. Chebotarev’s theorem turns these residue conditions into a square in a cubic number field, where traces restrict the numerator to two polynomials. A four-term calculation modulo seven excludes both. Section 3 follows these two stages: first extract the polynomial, then test whether it can satisfy the exact recurrence.

For the recurrence criteria we use the integer tail numerators of Koizumi [10]. In Section 4, a stable gcd and the Chinese remainder theorem force eventual Sylvester behaviour for a rational tail whose quotient 𝑎1⋯𝑎𝑛−1/𝑎𝑛a1⋯an−1/an has bounded upward increments. The separate summability criterion of Section 5 needs only integer increments and positivity. For the weighted criterion of Section 6, we instead clear tails by a least common multiple and use the denominator recurrence to control first crossings of new heights. Its convergence hypothesis is not supplied by the general quadratic limit. The companion paper also treats nonintegral rates and proves a stronger cubic disagreement theorem. Its detailed proof locations and the formal sources are listed in Appendix B.

Tail numerators

For the Sylvester sequence 2,3,7,43,…2,3,7,43,…, whose reciprocal sum is 11, the successive tails are 1,1/2,1/6,1/42,…1,1/2,1/6,1/42,…. Multiplication by the products 1,2,6,42,…1,2,6,42,… leaves the constant integer numerator 11. For any rational reciprocal sum, including a denominator of the whole sum in these products again gives integer numerators. We keep these fractions unreduced: the exact multiplicative denominator update will transfer the growth rate to the numerator.

Assume now that 𝑎𝑛an are strictly increasing positive integers, 𝑎𝑛+1/𝑎2𝑛 →1an+1/an2→1, and ∑𝑛≥11/𝑎𝑛 =𝑝/𝑞∑n≥11/an=p/q with positive integers 𝑝,𝑞p,q. All indices in this construction start at 11. Put

Proof of cubic-rate irrationality

Suppose, towards a contradiction, that the reciprocal sum in Theorem 1.2 is rational. Construct 𝐶𝑛,𝐷𝑛Cn,Dn as in Section 2. Equation (2) transfers the rate without changing its precision:

𝐶𝑛+1𝐶𝑛=1+3𝑛+𝑜(𝑛−3).(3)(3)Cn+1Cn=1+3n+o(n−3).

The ratio controls the error in a cubic approximation. The denominator recurrence will be used only after that approximation has become an exact polynomial.

Reduction and the constant term

We now use the denominator recurrence. Both updates preserve common divisors, so 𝐺𝑛 =gcd(𝐶𝑛,𝐷𝑛)Gn=gcd(Cn,Dn) forms a divisibility chain: 𝐺𝑛 ∣𝐺𝑛+1Gn∣Gn+1. For every sufficiently late 𝑛n, it divides four consecutive values of 𝐶𝑛Cn, hence their third difference 6𝐴6A. This is a fixed positive integer. The fourth difference identified the polynomial; the nonzero third difference now bounds a divisibility chain. Consequently 𝐺𝑛Gn stabilises at a positive integer 𝑔g.

We can therefore reduce all sufficiently late fractions by the same factor: put 𝑢𝑛 =𝐶𝑛/𝑔un=Cn/g and 𝑣𝑛 =𝐷𝑛/𝑔vn=Dn/g. The recurrences persist after this division. The following observation describes the resulting coprimality conditions.

Proposition 3.1 (persistent coprimality). Let 𝑎𝑛,𝑢𝑛,𝑣𝑛an,un,vn be integer sequences with 𝑢𝑛 >0un>0, 𝑣𝑛 ≥0vn≥0 and gcd(𝑢𝑛,𝑣𝑛) =1gcd(un,vn)=1 satisfying

𝑢𝑛+1=𝑎𝑛𝑢𝑛−𝑣𝑛,𝑣𝑛+1=𝑎𝑛𝑣𝑛.un+1=anun−vn,vn+1=anvn.

Then gcd(𝑎𝑛,𝑣𝑛) =1gcd(an,vn)=1. The 𝑎𝑛an are pairwise coprime, and gcd(𝑎𝑖,𝑢𝑡) =1gcd(ai,ut)=1 whenever 𝑖 <𝑡i<t.

Proof. A prime dividing both 𝑎𝑛an and 𝑣𝑛vn would divide 𝑢𝑛+1un+1 and 𝑣𝑛+1vn+1, contrary to reducedness. For 𝑖 <𝑡i<t, the factor 𝑎𝑖ai divides 𝑣𝑡vt. Reducedness gives gcd(𝑎𝑖,𝑢𝑡) =1gcd(ai,ut)=1, and gcd(𝑎𝑡,𝑣𝑡) =1gcd(at,vt)=1 gives gcd(𝑎𝑖,𝑎𝑡) =1gcd(ai,at)=1. ◻

𝑄(𝑛)=𝑚6𝑛(𝑛+1)(𝑛+2)+𝑐.(5)(5)Q(n)=m6n(n+1)(n+2)+c.

The binomial form separates two facts: 𝑄Q is integer-valued, and its constant term 𝑐c is an integer. Adjacent coprimality now restricts 𝑐c. If a prime ℓℓ divides 𝑐c, choose an arbitrarily late 𝑛 ≡ −1(mod6ℓ)n≡−1(mod6ℓ). Both three-factor products contain 𝑛 +1n+1, so division by 66 leaves a factor ℓℓ, even for ℓ =2,3ℓ=2,3. Thus ℓℓ divides both 𝑄(𝑛)Q(n) and 𝑄(𝑛 +1)Q(n+1), contradicting adjacent coprimality. This also excludes 𝑐 =0c=0. Thus

𝑚∈ℕ>0,𝑐∈{1,−1}.m∈N>0,c∈{1,−1}.

We also need irreducibility. The multipliers 𝑎𝑛 >1an>1 on the reduced tail are pairwise coprime, so infinitely many distinct primes occur among them. Once a prime divides one such 𝑎𝑛an, it divides every later 𝑣𝑡vt and no later 𝑢𝑡ut. If the cubic 𝑄Q had a rational root, that root would reduce to a root modulo all but finitely many primes. Choose one of the persistent primes outside those exceptions; a sufficiently late index in the root’s residue class would have ℓ ∣𝑄(𝑡) =𝑢𝑡ℓ∣Q(t)=ut, a contradiction. Section 2 of the companion proves positive lower density of disagreement with each rational cubic of this form. That lower bound depends on the orbit and the cubic. For Theorem 1.2, exclusion of eventual equality suffices.

Bounded increases

We return to the rational tails of Section 2. The Sylvester example had a constant integer numerator. To measure departure from this behaviour, put

Proposition 4.5 (gcd stabilisation). Let 𝑎,𝐶,𝐷 :ℕ →ℕa,C,D:N→N satisfy 𝑎𝑛 >1an>1, 𝐶𝑛 >0Cn>0 and (1). There are two distinct uses of the bound. Arbitrarily late negative errors in a fixed interval suffice to stabilise the gcd. The crossing argument below needs every sufficiently late upward step bounded; otherwise a single large rise could jump over the forbidden block.

A sequence avoiding multiples of 22 and 33 cannot cross the pair 6𝑘 +2,6𝑘 +36k+2,6k+3 from below with upward steps at most two: its first value at least 6𝑘 +26k+2 would be one of those two integers. Decreases before that crossing do not help. For a general step bound 𝐵B, the Chinese remainder theorem supplies a forbidden block of length 𝐵B.

Lemma 4.6 (consecutive multiples). For pairwise coprime integers 𝑚0,…,𝑚𝐵−1 ≥2m0,…,mB−1≥2 and every lower bound, there is a larger 𝑡t such that 𝑚𝑖 ∣𝑡 +𝑖mi∣t+i for each 𝑖 <𝐵i<B.

Finite total relative increase

Summable relative increases bound 𝐶𝑛Cn by an infinite product; discreteness then forces stationarity. No denominator recurrence is needed. Mere convergence of the relative increases to zero would allow both 𝐶𝑛 =𝑛 +1Cn=n+1 and 𝐶𝑛 =(𝑛 +1)2Cn=(n+1)2.

The companion’s Section 13 gives the details.

On an exact reciprocal-tail orbit the conclusion gives the Sylvester recurrence. For the gap sequence of the pseudo-greedy expansion, the same criterion, with the same product bound and integer descent, appears in the Erdős Problem a Day working report on Problem #243, dated 12 August 2026 [8]; the statement above is for any positive integer sequence with 𝐶𝑛+1 =𝐶𝑛 −𝐸𝑛Cn+1=Cn−En. This summability condition and the bound in Theorem 4.1 are different estimates. For exact reciprocal tails with |𝐸𝑛|/𝐶𝑛 →0|En|/Cn→0, each is equivalent to eventual vanishing of 𝐸𝑛En; neither estimate has been derived here from the unrestricted problem.

for some 𝐵B. This is a reformulation of the extra hypothesis, not a proof of it from quadratic growth. Both series use the full jump 𝑈𝑛+1 −𝑈𝑛Un+1−Un, including recovery from earlier decreases. Replacing it by 𝑅𝑛+1 −𝑅𝑛Rn+1−Rn, or merely proving that individual summands tend to zero, would not establish the required finiteness.

Corollary 6.2 (a bound using the least common multiple). Assume the hypotheses of Problem 1.1. Write 𝐴𝑛 =lcm⁡(𝑎1,…,𝑎𝑛−1)An=lcm⁡(a1,…,an−1) with 𝐴1 =1A1=1. If

lim sup𝑛→∞𝐴𝑛𝑎𝑛(𝑎2𝑛𝑎𝑛+1−1)<∞,lim supn→∞Anan(an2an+1−1)<∞,

then the sequence is eventually Sylvester.

Proof. Since 𝐿𝑛/𝐴𝑛 =𝑞/gcd(𝑞,𝐴𝑛)Ln/An=q/gcd(q,An) lies in [1,𝑞][1,q], an upper bound on the expression in the corollary gives an upper bound on (𝐿𝑛/𝑎𝑛)(𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1 −1)(Ln/an)(an2/an+1−1); negative terms remain negative. Equation (10) therefore bounds the negative part of 𝑉𝑛Vn. Choose an integer 𝐵B above that eventual bound. The record series then vanishes after a finite prefix, so Theorem 6.1 applies. ◻

The expression in Erdős and Straus’s Theorem 3 is

[𝑎1,…,𝑎𝑘]𝑎𝑘+1(𝑎2𝑘+1𝑎𝑘+2−1),[a1,…,ak]ak+1(ak+12ak+2−1),

with a nonpositive upper limit [1]. Setting 𝑛 =𝑘 +1n=k+1 gives exactly (𝐴𝑛/𝑎𝑛)𝛾𝑛(An/an)γn: the prefix ends before 𝑎𝑛an, and the growth ratio begins at 𝑎𝑛an. Tijdeman and Yuan extend this type of criterion to positive numerators [4]. Here any finite upper bound suffices under the quadratic-limit assumption. Since 𝐴𝑛 ∣𝑃𝑛An∣Pn, the LCM hypothesis is no stronger than the product hypothesis in Corollary 4.9: if the product expression is at most 𝐵B, the LCM expression is at most max(𝐵,0)max(B,0). When the earlier terms are pairwise coprime the two weights agree; repeated prime factors can make the LCM much smaller. This comparison does not assert the existence of a non-Sylvester rational example satisfying one bound but not the other.

The finite upper limit means an eventual upper bound; it does not require 𝑞q to divide the LCM of the preceding denominators. For positive integer summand numerators 𝑏𝑛bn, the modified error is 𝑉𝑛 =𝑏𝑛𝐿𝑛 −(𝑎𝑛 −1)𝑈𝑛Vn=bnLn−(an−1)Un. The companion, Section 6 under “Integer coefficients”, separately proves boundedness from a lower bound on 𝑉𝑛Vn and eventual constancy when 𝑉𝑛/𝑈𝑛 →0Vn/Un→0 is also assumed. The latter conclusion must not be read into the first hypothesis alone. The same section links finite examples separating them; compare Badea [3] and Tijdeman–Yuan [4]. The companion’s Section 3 compares Duverney’s signed-series criterion [2], whose printed condition is one-sided, with the stronger absolute-convergence specialisation used there. It also records the different growth hypotheses for irrationality exponents in [14]. Neither comparison is an input to the crossing theorem.

Further questions

Proposition 7.1 (necessary profile). The integer tail of a sequence satisfying Problem 1.1’s hypotheses but not its conclusion has 𝐸𝑛 ≠0En≠0 eventually, |𝐸𝑛|/𝐶𝑛 →0|En|/Cn→0, unbounded negative magnitudes along negative indices, and

∑𝑛(−𝐸𝑛)+𝐶𝑛=∞.∑n(−En)+Cn=∞.

Proof. Absorption excludes late zeros, descent excludes an eventually nonnegative error, and Theorems 4.1 and 5.1 exclude the two finiteness conditions. ◻

For 𝐵 ≥0B≥0 put

𝐹𝐵(𝑋)=∑𝑛∈R𝑈𝑛≤𝑋(−𝑉𝑛−𝐵)+.FB(X)=∑n∈RUn≤X(−Vn−B)+.

This groups record steps by their starting numerator 𝑈𝑛Un, not by time or by the running maximum. To apply the weighted criterion without guessing a weight, it would suffice to prove from growth and rationality that, for some fixed integer 𝐵 ≥0B≥0,

lim inf𝑋→∞𝐹𝐵(𝑋)𝑋=0.(13)(13)lim infX→∞FB(X)X=0.

If the recurrence is not eventually Sylvester, first crossings instead give 𝐹𝐵(𝑋) ≥𝑋/𝑃𝐵 −𝑂𝐵(1)FB(X)≥X/PB−OB(1), with an orbit-dependent CRT modulus 𝑃𝐵PB. In that case 𝑈𝑛 →∞Un→∞, so only finitely many record steps begin below a fixed 𝑋X. The next lemma explains why one may seek (13) instead of choosing a weight in advance: enumerate the record indices by 𝑗j and set 𝑢𝑗 =𝑈𝑛uj=Un, 𝑤𝑗 =( −𝑉𝑛 −𝐵)+wj=(−Vn−B)+. A vanishing lower ratio supplies an admissible weight with a finite series. Proving that ratio estimate would therefore contradict the crossing lower bound and exclude every non-Sylvester rational tail.

Then lim inf𝑋→∞𝐹(𝑋)/𝑋 =0lim infX→∞F(X)/X=0 if and only if there is a finite nonincreasing 𝑓 :[1,∞) →[0,∞)f:[1,∞)→[0,∞) with ∫∞1𝑓(𝑡) 𝑑𝑡 =∞∫1∞f(t)dt=∞ and ∑𝑗𝑤𝑗𝑓(𝑢𝑗) <∞∑jwjf(uj)<∞.

Arithmetic compatibility

The remaining estimate requires the denominator recurrence as well as control of the error. For example, 𝐶𝑛 =𝑛2 +1Cn=n2+1, 𝐸𝑛 = −(2𝑛 +1)En=−(2n+1) has vanishing relative error and the necessary scalar pattern. But at 𝑛 =2,3,4n=2,3,4 its numerators are 5,10,175,10,17. The update 10 =5𝑎2 −𝐷210=5a2−D2 forces 5 ∣𝐷25∣D2, hence 5 ∣𝐷3 =𝑎2𝐷25∣D3=a2D2; the next update would force 5 ∣175∣17. Thus these numerators cannot satisfy (1). The companion’s Section 14 also constructs sequences avoiding sparse fixed moduli and distinguishes that avoidance from compatibility with all later denominators. Neither property alone supplies (13).

Conversely, suppose integer sequences indexed from zero satisfy (1), with 𝑎𝑛 >1an>1, 𝐶𝑛 >0Cn>0, 𝐷𝑛 ≥0Dn≥0 and 𝐸𝑛/𝐶𝑛 →0En/Cn→0. Section 4 of the companion proves that 𝐷𝑛 >0Dn>0, 𝐶𝑛/𝐷𝑛 →0Cn/Dn→0, ∑𝑛1/𝑎𝑛 =𝐶0/𝐷0∑n1/an=C0/D0 and 𝑎𝑛+1/𝑎2𝑛 →1an+1/an2→1. The vanishing remainder 𝐶𝑛/𝐷𝑛 →0Cn/Dn→0 turns the finite reciprocal identities into an infinite series. A scalar profile or finite prefix does not supply it.

Problem 7.3 (growth of repeated denominator factors). For every rational-tail orbit satisfying the hypotheses but not the conclusion of Problem 1.1, must

lim sup𝑛→∞log⁡𝑀𝑛𝑛>0?lim supn→∞log⁡Mnn>0?

Equivalently, must there be a 𝐾 ≥1K≥1 for which

2𝑛≤𝑀𝐾𝑛2n≤MnK

at infinitely many indices?

Section 2 gives 𝐶𝑛+1/𝐶𝑛 →1Cn+1/Cn→1; averaging logarithms therefore gives log⁡𝐶𝑛 =𝑜(𝑛)log⁡Cn=o(n). Since 1 ≤𝑀𝑛 ≤𝐶𝑛1≤Mn≤Cn, every such orbit already satisfies log⁡𝑀𝑛/𝑛 →0log⁡Mn/n→0. A positive answer therefore holds exactly when no such orbit exists: proving it from failure of Sylvester behaviour would exclude every counterexample.

A factorial modulus for integral recursion

A constant-negative error 𝐸𝑛 = −𝑚En=−m with 𝐶0 =𝑐C0=c gives 𝐶𝑛 =𝑐 +𝑛𝑚Cn=c+nm and the identity

𝐷𝑛+𝑚=(𝑎𝑛−1)𝐶𝑛.(14)(14)Dn+m=(an−1)Cn.

In the case 𝑚 =𝑐 =1m=c=1, where (14) reads 𝐷𝑛 +1 =(𝑎𝑛 −1)(𝑛 +1)Dn+1=(an−1)(n+1), each multiplier is determined by its predecessor. The recursion is 𝑎𝑛+1 =num⁡(𝑛,𝑎𝑛)/(𝑛 +2)an+1=num⁡(n,an)/(n+2), where

num⁡(𝑛,𝑎)=(𝑛+1)𝑎2−(𝑛+2)𝑎+(𝑛+3),num⁡(n,a)=(n+1)a2−(n+2)a+(n+3),

the forced numerator. We stop at the first nonintegral quotient. This procedure checks divisibility only; it does not impose the positivity conditions required of an infinite reciprocal-tail sequence. The formal exact-division condition requires exact division at each step.

Example A.1 (a nonintegral second step). Starting from 𝑎0 =3a0=3, the first numerator num⁡(0,3) =6num⁡(0,3)=6 is divisible by 22, giving 𝑎1 =3a1=3. The next numerator num⁡(1,3) =13num⁡(1,3)=13 is not divisible by 33, so the recursion stops.

Direct iteration can produce very large intermediate integers. To decide whether the first ℎh divisions are exact, however, it suffices to know the initial value modulo (ℎ +1)!(h+1)!. Computing a pseudo-greedy orbit through residues modulo a shrinking product modulus is Koizumi’s method [10]; for the forced numerator that product is a factorial.

Theorem A.2 (factorial residue reduction). Let ℎh be a nonnegative integer and let 𝑎,𝑏a,b be integers with 𝑎 ≡𝑏(mod(ℎ +1)!)a≡b(mod(h+1)!). The first ℎh steps of the recursion 𝑎𝑛+1 =num⁡(𝑛,𝑎𝑛)/(𝑛 +2)an+1=num⁡(n,an)/(n+2), starting at index zero, are integral for 𝑎0 =𝑎a0=a if and only if they are integral for 𝑎0 =𝑏a0=b.

Proof. Each exact division consumes a congruence factor. Accordingly, define 𝑀(0,𝑖) =1M(0,i)=1 and 𝑀(ℎ +1,𝑖) =(𝑖 +2)𝑀(ℎ,𝑖 +1)M(h+1,i)=(i+2)M(h,i+1). Thus 𝑀(ℎ,0) =(ℎ +1)!M(h,0)=(h+1)!. We prove the stronger statement that, at index 𝑖i, congruent inputs modulo 𝑀(ℎ,𝑖)M(h,i) give the same answer to whether the next ℎh quotients are all integral. There is nothing to prove for ℎ =0h=0.

For the inductive step, suppose 𝑎 ≡𝑏(mod(𝑖 +2)𝑀(ℎ,𝑖 +1))a≡b(mod(i+2)M(h,i+1)). Since num⁡(𝑖, ⋅)num⁡(i,⋅) is an integer polynomial, its values at 𝑎a and 𝑏b are congruent modulo that product. In particular, one is divisible by 𝑖 +2i+2 if and only if the other is. If neither is divisible, both recursions stop. Otherwise their quotients are congruent modulo 𝑀(ℎ,𝑖 +1)M(h,i+1), so the induction hypothesis applies to the remaining ℎh updates at index 𝑖 +1i+1. Taking 𝑖 =0i=0 proves the claim. ◻

For ℎ =1h=1, the condition is 2 ∣𝑎2 −2𝑎 +32∣a2−2a+3, or equivalently that 𝑎a is odd. This illustrates Theorem A.2 with modulus 2! =22!=2.

The enumeration in Example 9.1 of the companion, over 2 ≤𝑎0 <50002≤a0<5000, gives at most 1717 successful updates (1818 values including 𝑎0a0). The seed 𝑎0 =1a0=1 is excluded because it is fixed and violates 𝑎𝑛 ≥2an≥2. This finite calculation establishes only the stated range. The infinite constant-negative exclusion requires the separate argument under the hypotheses given there.

Sources and related work

The companion Reciprocal Sums and the Sylvester Recurrence: Further Results and Proofs supplies full proofs and fixed-revision links: Section 2 for regular rates and cubic disagreement; Sections 4–5 for integer tails; Section 12 for the gcd and bounded-increment arguments; Section 6 for LCM results; Section 13 for scalar summability; and Section 14 for open estimates and failed constructions. A final map records dependencies. The auxiliary constructions satisfy only their stated hypotheses, not necessarily those of a rational reciprocal series.

For the earlier integer-remainder method see Erdős–Straus [12]. The companion’s Section 3 distinguishes polynomial Cantor series [13] and the freely selectable series of Problem #270 [15] from the present setting. The Isabelle/HOL work [16] formalises older Erdős–Straus criteria, not Problem #243. General-rate extraction uses the Gamma-ratio asymptotics in [17]; the cubic case uses the explicit 𝐹𝑛Fn.

Indexing of the canonical tails.

Section 2 starts with 𝐶1 =𝑝C1=p, 𝐷1 =𝑞D1=q. Setting 𝑎0 =1a0=1, 𝐷0 =𝑞D0=q, 𝐶0 =𝑝 +𝑞C0=p+q extends the recurrences by one update, but gives neither 𝑎0 >1a0>1 nor strict increase at that step. The zero-based formal cubic theorem instead uses 𝑁N with 𝑎𝑁 >𝑁aN>N, 𝑏𝑛 =𝑛 +1bn=n+1 for 0 ≤𝑛 <𝑁0≤n<N and 𝑏𝑛 =𝑎𝑛bn=an thereafter. This sequence is strictly increasing and changes the reciprocal sum by a rational finite sum without shifting 𝑛n or 3/𝑛3/n on the tail. See the companion’s indexing subsection.

Verification and reproducibility

The links identify fixed-revision Lean declarations and recorded Comparator checks. The printed cubic argument uses Chebotarev; the formal square-specialisation proof uses a Dedekind-zeta pole comparison. Their common conclusion does not check each step of the printed proof. This revision includes no new Lean build, Comparator replay or independent review. The evidence record retains source-pin and index gaps, and the estimate in Section 7 remains open.

The formal factorial residue reduction uses the shrinking-modulus induction, polynomial congruence, and cancellation after exact division. Its modulus is identified by the ascending-factorial formula and its factorial value at the initial index.

What is checked in Lean
  • Lean proves cubic_rate_irrationality_unconditional for positive StrictMono zero-indexed 𝑎𝑛an with 𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1 =1 +3/𝑛 +𝑜(𝑛−3)an2/an+1=1+3/n+o(n−3). The one-based paper uses a finite-prefix bridge; general #243 remains open.
  • Lean proves nonintegral_regular_rate_irrational for positive StrictMono zero-indexed 𝑎𝑛an whenever the real coefficient lambda is greater than one and nonintegral, with 𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1 =1an2/an+1=1 + lambda/n + 𝑜(𝑛−𝜆)o(n−λ). Summability is derived. The one-based paper uses the same finite-prefix bridge; the unrestricted problem remains open.
  • The exact product-cleared tail dynamics and the defect identity, as identities in the integer state variables.
  • That a vanishing centred state is absorbing under strict centring, so the state is either eventually zero or nowhere zero.
  • That eventual vanishing of the centred state, with the next tail state nonvanishing, forces the Sylvester recurrence eventually.
  • That a nonnegative centred state vanishes eventually, by descent.
  • That the centred state cannot be eventually constant and negative, at any magnitude and any common scale.
  • That the negative magnitude cannot be eventually periodic with positive drift, in the regime where each magnitude is below its multiplier.
  • A coprimality barrier: a sequence tending to infinity with uniformly bounded upward increments cannot permanently avoid infinitely many fresh pairwise coprime moduli.
  • That a reduced exact tail has pairwise coprime multipliers which its numerator permanently avoids, so no such tail has a divergent numerator with bounded rise.
  • That the tail gcd stabilises under cofinally bounded negative magnitudes.
  • Conditionally: exact dynamics, eventual strict centring, an eventually bounded negative part, and normalised vanishing together force the centred state to vanish eventually.
  • That survival through a fixed number of forced updates depends only on the initial state modulo a factorial of the horizon.
  • From a strictly increasing positive integer sequence, a rational reciprocal sum and 𝑎𝑛+1/𝑎2𝑛an+1/an2 tending to one, canonical_integer_tail_normalized derives eventual strict centring and normalised vanishing of the exact integer tail.
What is not checked
  • The unrestricted problem.
  • A uniform lower bound on the centred error for every sequence in the original problem; the canonical tail transfer does not supply this additional hypothesis.
  • Any exclusion of negative excursions whose magnitudes are unbounded along a cofinal set.
  • The Erdős–Straus weighted criterion and Duverney's conditional characterisation, which are cited rather than formalised here.
The formal record: 4 main results, 3 open obligations, 9 selected result modules, finite search evidence, Comparator review

Main results

Statements and boundaries are copied from the corpus record. Registry status: registered_declarations

conditional reduction and no-go result family: bounded_negative_exclusion

ErdosProblems.Erdos243.no_cofinallyBoundedNegative_of_normalizedVanishes
locally proved signed recovery/rigidity theorem; novelty unassessed family: centered_state_dynamics

Under exact natural C/D dynamics with 𝑎 >1,𝐶 >0,𝐸 =𝐷a>1,C>0,E=D - (a - 1)C, strict |E| <𝐶<C, a uniform lower bound on E, and division-free normalized vanishing, boundedNegativePart_eventually_zero forces 𝐸 =0E=0 eventually; centered-zero plus an eventually nonzero next tail recovers eventual Sylvester recurrence.

The signed theorem has a C D : ℕ → ℕ, E : ℕ → ℤ, and B : ℕ with all exact hypotheses explicit: 𝑎 >1,𝐶 >0a>1,C>0, C(n + 1) + D(n) = a(n) · C(n), D(n + 1) = a(n) · D(n), E is the centered state D − (a − 1)C, |E| <𝐶<C, a uniform lower bound on E, and division-free normalized vanishing. It excludes persistent bounded negative behaviour and forces eventual centered defect zero; centered-zero plus an eventually nonzero next tail recovers Sylvester, but no reciprocal-tail irrationality follows. The unbounded negative mixed-sign branch and the prime-specific producer remain open. This is distinct from the periodic negative-orbit and cofinally bounded-negative no-go families; no novelty, priority, significance, or external-review claim is made, and no unrestricted #243 solution follows.

ErdosProblems.Erdos243.boundedNegativePart_eventually_zero
conditional analytic recovery criterion; novelty unassessed family: negative_mass_recovery

Under exact next-denominator and next-tail C/D dynamics with a, D : ℕ → ℤ, C : ℕ → ℕ, 𝐶 >0C>0, the strict centered step equation, division-free normalized vanishing, and Summable normalized negative centered mass, the centered state vanishes eventually and a follows the Sylvester recurrence eventually.

This is a conditional recovery criterion: the source theorem assumes every displayed dynamics, positivity, strict centered-step, normalized-vanishing, and summability hypothesis, and does not prove them for the original Erdős #243 orbit. Any surviving canonical orbit must have divergent normalized negative mass. It supplies no prime-specific producer, unconditional #243 endpoint, or reciprocal-tail irrationality, and makes no novelty, priority, significance, or external-review claim. It is distinct from centered_state_dynamics, which uses a uniform lower-bound hypothesis rather than summability of normalized negative mass.

ErdosProblems.Erdos243.sylvesterNext_eventually_of_summable_negativeRelativeMass
no-go result family: negative_orbit_no_go

An eventually periodic negative-error orbit with positive phase growth is impossible.

The theorem does not cover arbitrary unbounded negative behaviour.

ErdosProblems.Erdos243.no_eventuallyPeriodicNegative_orbit

Open obligations

Prove any one of these and the corresponding reduction above becomes unconditional.

  • unbounded_negative_excursions Exclude or construct exact orbits with infinitely many unbounded negative centred excursions. Checked exclusions assume bounded negative part, a fixed period, or fixed prime divisors.
  • derive_negative_part_bound Derive a lower bound on centred error from the original growth and rational-sum hypotheses, control unbounded negative excursions another way, or construct a counterexample.
  • formalise_the_published_criteria Kernel-check the Erdos-Straus weighted criterion and Duverney's conditional characterisation under explicit analytic hypotheses.

Finite search evidence

An exact search over initial states below five thousand produced forced prefixes of length seventeen and no longer. It is superseded: the constant-negative template is now excluded outright, for every seed and at every scale.
